claims.claim: Health equity is the state in which everyone has a fair and just opportunity to attain their highest level of health; achieving it requires focused and ongoing societal efforts to address historical and contemporary injustices, overcome economic, social, and other obstacles to health and health care, and eliminate preventable health disparities.

Healthy People 2030, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' national public health goals, defines health equity as the attainment of the highest level of health for all people, which requires valuing everyone equally with focused and ongoing societal efforts to address avoidable inequalities, historical and contemporary injustices, and social determinants of health, and to eliminate disparities in health and health care.

The World Health Organization defines equity as the absence of unfair, avoidable or remediable differences among groups of people, and states that health equity is achieved when everyone can attain their full potential for health and well-being.

Health disparities are measurable health differences between groups of people, including how many people get certain diseases, how severe the diseases are, how many die, whether people can get health care, and how many get screened; groups may be defined by race, ethnicity, income, education, geography, sex, gender, and other characteristics.

Health inequities arise from systems that create and reinforce barriers preventing individuals and communities from accessing the conditions needed to reach their full potential; inequities differ from health disparities, which are measurable differences in health outcomes between groups, and disparities are one way to assess progress toward health equity.

Measuring health disparities is essential to advancing health equity; Healthy People 2030 monitors differences across population groups and features evidence-based interventions and multisector collaborations as tools for action.

Health equity is pursued by transforming the systems and structures that create inequities, valuing all people equally, optimizing the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, learn, and age, and collaborating across sectors such as employment, housing, education, health care, and food access.

Realizing the right to health is a progressive, ongoing process of systematically identifying and eliminating inequities that result from differences in health and living conditions, rather than a single one-time fix.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The wording of the working definition differs across agencies
positions: HHS/Healthy People 2030: health equity is the attainment of the highest level of health for all people
CDC: health equity is the state in which everyone has a fair and just opportunity to attain their highest level of health
WHO: health equity is achieved when everyone can attain their full potential for health and well-being
APHA: everyone has the opportunity to attain their highest level of health
conflictingEvidence.resolution: All four formulations share the same core idea — a fair opportunity for everyone to be healthy. The lesson presents the fair-and-just-opportunity formulation as the working definition (the wording used by U.S. government health agencies) and notes the family of definitions from WHO and APHA.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Equality and equity are sometimes used interchangeably in everyday speech
positions: Some discussions treat equal treatment for everyone as the fairness goal

Public health agencies distinguish equity from equality: equity emphasizes fair outcomes and removing barriers (CDC: overcoming economic, social, and other obstacles; APHA: transforming systems that create barriers), which can require different levels of support for different groups
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the standard distinction — equality gives everyone the same thing; equity aims for fair outcomes by removing barriers — using original examples, and attributes the barrier-removal framing to the CDC and APHA.

Kept the lesson inside its lane: specific disparity statistics and trends belong to the health-disparities sibling topic; the social-determinants framework belongs to its sibling; policy instruments belong to public-health-policy. This lesson states the equity goal, the equity/equality distinction, and how equity is pursued without drifting into those topics.
rightsIssues: None. HHS/health.gov, CDC, and MedlinePlus are U.S. government works (public domain, attributed). WHO and APHA pages are used as reference only, with facts synthesized in original wording and no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Health Equity in Healthy People 2030
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (Healthy People 2030)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20241004151250 of the live URL (health.gov direct fetch returned 404; capture dated 2024-10-04). Supports: Healthy People 2030's definition of health equity as the attainment of the highest level of health for all people, requiring valuing everyone equally with focused and ongoing societal efforts to address avoidable inequalities, historical and contemporary injustices, and social determinants of health, and to eliminate disparities in health and health care; the overarching goal 'Eliminate health disparities, achieve health equity, and attain health literacy to improve the health and well-being of all'; the definition of a health disparity as a health difference closely linked with social, economic, and/or environmental disadvantage; the statement that measuring health disparities is essential to advancing health equity; and the Tools for Action framing (objectives, data, evidence-based resources, and Healthy People in Action stories of multisector collaboration).

CDC sub-topics (minority health, women's health, racism and health) listed on the page are not developed in this lesson.
